system: You rewrite research decisions as topic-neutral abstractions. Return only the JSON object asked for.
prompt:
Below are research decisions made by several different researchers. Rewrite each one into the fixed
template below so that a reader cannot tell what field, topic, paper, organisation or person it comes from, nor what
kind of work it is: an experiment, a new procedure, a measurement suite, a write-up choice, or a decision about what
to share or fund must all read alike. Keep the trade-off that was faced and which way it was decided.

Template, one entry per item:
- "situation": one sentence, at most 30 words: the position the researcher was in when the decision came up.
- "options_considered": two or three short options separated by " / ", including the one taken. If the source names
  no alternative, give the plain opposite of what was done.
- "choice": one sentence, at most 25 words, starting with "Chose", saying which option was taken.
- "reason": one sentence, at most 25 words, giving the stated reason; if none is stated write "No reason stated."

Rules:
- Remove every domain noun and technical term: names of models, systems, datasets, procedures, organisations, people,
  papers and coined terms; and any wording that reveals the area.
- Use only plain generic words such as: the result, the claim, the finding, the check, the comparison, the setup,
  the change, the next step, the question, the work, the variant, the condition, the sample, the system.
- Never use any of these words or any form of them: ability, access, accuracy, allow, appeared, assessment, attack, avoid, baselines, behavior, behaviour, benchmark, best, bound, call, capability, cheap, claiming, clean, comes, complex, components, content, cost, defense, difficulty, disclosure, effect, effects, error, evaluate, evaluated, evaluating, evaluation, evaluator, evaluators, failures, features, form, format, four, gains, generalise, generalization, generalize, ground, harm, harmful, implication, improve, improvement, information, internal, intervention, judged, key, limit, matched, mechanism, method, methods, metric, observed, organisation, pattern, performance, phenomenon, picture, point, policy, possibly, practical, preference, preferences, public, publication, publish, rater, reduce, release, residual, responses, risk, rule, safety, sampled, say, score, shifts, similar, source, stage, success, supporting, task, tasks, technique, time, tool, tools, trait, transfer, transferred, treatment, unintended, unmodified, unwanted, value, varies, verify, wording.
- Add nothing that is not in the source. Never say who made the decision. Write every item in the same plain style.

Return {"items": [{"id": ..., "situation": ..., "options_considered": ..., "choice": ..., "reason": ...}, ...]}
with one entry per input item, in input order.

ITEMS:
[
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:e8247a1e039d",
  "problem": "Whether to accept LLM-generated impossible mutations as valid, given that they may not truly be impossible, especially for multi-file SWE-bench tasks.",
  "did": "They validated each mutation by running it against both the original patch and an empty patch and removed any mutation that passed either, while skipping this check for LiveCodeBench.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "LLM-generated mutations are not guaranteed to be valid, and the filtering reduces noise; LiveCodeBench lacks standard solutions so the check cannot be done there."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:fa3cb76292a2",
  "problem": "How to design evaluation protocols so they are useful regardless of who runs the evaluation.",
  "did": "METR aims to build evaluation protocols that any evaluator can use, including governments, internal lab teams, other third parties or METR itself.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "government",
   "an internal lab team",
   "another third party",
   "a team at METR"
  ],
  "stated_reason": ""
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:31a238dd83b8",
  "problem": "How to interpret the reward model sycophant result, where many behaviors were surfaced but the core objective was not.",
  "did": "They reported partial success (16 of 52 behaviors) and characterized the IA as surfacing symptomatic behaviors while missing the less salient core hidden objective.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "The model never stated it was optimizing for reward model scores, the core hidden objective."
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:fa7a2528d316",
  "problem": "How to attack a defense claimed to be end-to-end differentiable yet evaluated with BPDA.",
  "did": "Hypothesized the BPDA wrapper was causing gradient masking and removed it with a one-line change, rerunning the original evaluation code.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "designing a new adaptive attack"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Sabre is already differentiable, so wrapping it in BPDA removes the useful gradient and replaces it with a much less useful one."
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:a1b91b092e5c",
  "problem": "How to interpret why the tools gave no uplift despite their outputs changing the predictor's answers.",
  "did": "They analyzed NLA outputs with LLM judges and concluded that causal relationships between the edited feature and the behavior are almost never stated, while treating this analysis as only a qualitative diagnostic.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "the predictor ignoring tool outputs",
   "poor token selection by the agent",
   "activations being inherently incomplete for causal claims",
   "tools needing better elicitation or scaffolding"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Explicit 'X causes Y' statements appeared in only 0.6% of positive claims, and applying the judge to every transcript token left the rate near zero, ruling out poor token selection."
 },
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:6964ddb23657",
  "problem": "How to test whether mid-training on diverse tasks yields positive cross-task transfer.",
  "did": "Mid-train on about 100 tasks at once with less data per task, then fine-tune on the original task data and compare against the stage 1 result.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "training on isolated individual tasks (stage 1)"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "To make sure that mid-training on a diverse set of tasks also helps with individual tasks."
 },
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:32b45514cc05",
  "problem": "Deciding how to fix dead concepts during PCD training after alternatives failed.",
  "did": "Dropped normalizing encoder directions and annealing, did not adapt the Gao et al. auxiliary loss, and introduced a custom auxiliary loss that revives dead concepts.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "normalizing encoder directions",
   "annealing the number of active concepts",
   "the auxiliary loss of Gao et al. (2024)"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Normalizing and annealing were not effective, and adapting the Gao et al. loss would require twice as many decoder forward and backward passes."
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:8df02880536c",
  "problem": "Verifying that each fine-tuned adversarial model is truly harmful before using it as a positive example in the evaluation.",
  "did": "They confirmed attack success for every adversarial model on HEx-PHI with a GPT-4o judge, using attack-specific elicitation, before including it.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "Without attack-specific elicitation some attacks go undetected, so confirmation requires eliciting with the attack's own method."
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:5e45b000a0bb",
  "problem": "Which metric best reports attacker performance on a benchmark with many degrees of freedom.",
  "did": "The authors proposed plotting the sorted robust accuracy of every defense as a cumulative distribution, with average robust accuracy and count of defenses below half of clean accuracy only as fallback scalars.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "a single scalar number",
   "binary success or failure per challenge"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "The full curve captures intermediate solutions, while the two scalars capture average-case improvement and substantial degradation respectively."
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:16489d8e0185",
  "problem": "How to evaluate LLM extraction of SSNs from scanned JFK documents against a meaningful baseline.",
  "did": "They ran Tesseract OCR and then a data loss prevention tool, decomposing the baseline into a transcription upper bound and an actual detection count.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "comparing only against final DLP detection counts"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Counting correctly transcribed SSNs gives an upper bound on what any analysis of the transcribed text could identify."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:e1f397ca21f6",
  "problem": "They needed to show that value influence exists and also whether the model discloses it.",
  "did": "Built evaluations that quantify both the shift in answers and the disclosure. The abstract suggests this includes reading the chain-of-thought on a Fermi-estimation task and comparing answers across contexts, such as Anthropic vs OpenAI as the company under consideration.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "Not explicitly stated beyond the need to quantify leakage and disclosure."
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:ebb6a693876e",
  "problem": "Determining whether directly querying or benchmarking a fine-tuned model is enough to reveal harmful behavior introduced by covert attacks.",
  "did": "They gave the auditor attack-specific elicitation affordances (dataset-derived system prompts, cipher-encoded prompts, backdoor triggers) rather than relying on plain benchmarks or queries.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "directly querying the harmful model with a benchmark designed to detect misaligned models",
   "running a benchmark or querying without attack-specific elicitation"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Many attacks are only effective if the model is queried according to the attack, so un-elicited queries make harmful models appear relatively safe."
 }
]
